V01-M-001: Our confidence that bread will nourish us tomorrow, or that the sun will rise, rests on an unstated premise: that the future will resemble the past. Logic cannot supply that premise, since there is no contradiction in supposing that nature might change its course tomorrow. Experience is no better placed, for to argue that the future will resemble the past because it always has done so is to assume the very premise in question. Faced with this dilemma, some philosophers have concluded that inductive inference is not rationally justified at all, but merely a habit of mind. A second response holds that the demand was misplaced from the start, since induction is part of what we mean by reasoning well and needs no deeper foundation.
V01-M-002: Slippery slope arguments warn that a modest step, harmless in itself, will lead by stages to an outcome that nobody wants. Such arguments are often dismissed as fallacies, but whether they fail depends on what is supposed to carry us down the slope, and two cases must be distinguished. If each step merely makes the next one conceivable, the warning is weak, since conceivability is cheap and most conceivable steps are never taken. If, however, each step changes the incentives or precedents that govern the next decision, the slope may be real and the warning deserves a hearing.
V01-M-003: An old parable describes a donkey placed exactly midway between two identical bales of hay, which starves because it has no reason to prefer either. The story is absurd as zoology, since any real animal would simply start eating, but it poses a genuine puzzle for theories of rational choice. Put abstractly, the puzzle is this: if rational agents act only on reasons, an agent facing two perfectly equal options seems to have no rational way to begin. The real animal's escape, an arbitrary choice, suggests that the capacity to pick without a reason is not a flaw in rationality but one of its necessary supports.
V01-M-004: One influential test in ethics asks whether the principle behind an action could be willed as a rule that everyone follows. A lying promise fails the test neatly: if everyone made promises they meant to break, nobody would accept a promise, and the lie could not even be told. Critics point out that the test seems to condemn harmless policies just as readily, such as playing tennis on Sunday mornings because the courts are empty, which would defeat itself if everyone did it. What the test needs, then, is a way of describing actions that separates the deceiver's principle from the tennis player's, and supplying it has proved harder than it first appears.
V01-M-005: Imagine a gym offering two memberships, a monthly plan and a much pricier annual one, and finding that most new members pick the monthly plan. The owner then introduces a six-month plan that costs almost as much as the annual membership. Hardly anyone signs up for the new six-month plan, but annual memberships climb, because the annual plan now looks generous beside its costly neighbour. Having done its work without being bought, the six-month plan is what marketers call a decoy, an option whose job is to flatter a rival placed beside it.
V01-M-006: Psychologists have long observed that an interrupted task tends to linger in the mind longer than one brought to completion. The interrupted task, whether a half-written letter or an unsolved puzzle, keeps returning to awareness, as though the mind were reluctant to let go of an unreached goal. This persistence can be useful, since a problem left open overnight is sometimes solved in the morning without further effort. It can also be a burden, as anyone who has lain awake rehearsing tomorrow's unfinished chores will know. The burden, interestingly, often lifts once a person writes down a concrete plan for completing the task, even before any of the work is done.
V01-M-007: People tend to credit their successes to their own ability and effort while blaming their failures on bad luck, unfair tests or difficult circumstances. At first sight this looks like simple vanity, a refusal to face unwelcome truths about oneself. Yet the habit may serve a purpose, because someone who reads every failure as proof of personal inadequacy may stop trying altogether. The bias, on this view, is less a defect of reasoning than a buffer that keeps people persisting long enough to improve.
V01-M-008: Most people know the frustration of a word that seems about to surface but refuses to appear, a state psychologists call being on the tip of the tongue. In this state, people can often report the first letter of the missing word, or how many syllables it has, though the word itself stays out of reach. Such partial knowledge suggests that retrieving a word happens in stages, with its meaning and its sound stored somewhat separately. When the state occurs, then, the meaning has been found but the route to the sound has briefly failed.
V01-M-009: Working memory can hold only a handful of separate items at once, which is why a long string of random digits is so hard to repeat. The limit, however, applies to the number of items, not to the amount of information each item carries. A chess master glancing at a board sees not twenty-odd pieces but a few familiar patterns, each of which counts as a single item. Expertise, on this account, does not enlarge memory so much as reorganise what is held in it into larger meaningful units.
V01-M-010: Children playing cricket in narrow lanes rarely follow the official laws of the game. Instead, they invent local rules suited to the space, such as declaring a batter out for hitting the ball into a neighbour's balcony. These rules are not arbitrary, since each one solves a practical problem that the particular lane presents, like a ball lost in a drain or a neighbour who complains. A lane's rulebook is therefore a small record of its problems, and so of the street's geography and of the people who live along it.
V01-M-011: For generations, the public library was defined by its rule of silence, enforced by stern notices and sterner librarians. Many libraries today have relaxed that rule, adding cafes, children's corners and rooms for group study. Some regular users complain that the change has destroyed the one public space where concentration was possible. Their complaint is not merely nostalgic, since homes and offices now offer fewer quiet places than they once did. The better answer, then, is not to restore silence everywhere but to protect it in some rooms while letting the rest of the building be noisy.
V01-M-012: Many extended families now keep in touch through a single group chat on their phones. Such a group lets distant cousins share news, photographs and birthday wishes without the effort of individual calls. The same group, however, can become a source of friction, as forwarded rumours and unwanted advice reach everyone at once. Many members respond by muting the chat, staying in it for the sake of family peace while rarely reading what is posted.
V01-M-013: The neighbourhood tea stall sells a cheap drink, but what keeps its customers coming back is the conversation around it. Strangers who would never visit one another's homes stand shoulder to shoulder there, exchanging news about jobs, prices and local disputes. They can mix so freely because the space belongs to nobody in particular, so no one has to play host and no one owes an invitation in return. It is this absence of obligation, more than the tea, that makes the stall a meeting place open to almost anyone.
V01-M-014: Citizens of classical Athens could, if they chose, hold a vote to send one prominent man into exile for ten years. Each voter scratched a name on a fragment of broken pottery, and the man named most often had to leave the city. Remarkably, the exile kept his property and his citizenship, and could return with full rights when the decade ended. The procedure was thus not a punishment for a crime but a way of removing a man whose influence had grown dangerous to the balance of the city. Its weakness was that the same tool could be turned against any rival whom a faction wished to be rid of, whether or not he posed a real threat.
V01-M-015: In many growing cities of the past, fires were fought by whoever happened to be nearby, with buckets passed from hand to hand. As property became more valuable, insurance companies began to employ their own teams of trained firefighters. These private brigades had an obvious interest in saving insured buildings, but fire rarely respects the boundaries of a policy. Over time, the case for a single public fire service, paid for by everyone and serving everyone, became hard to resist.
V01-M-016: Merchants who met at the great medieval fairs faced a problem that had little to do with goods: how to trust partners they might never see again. A cheated trader could hardly pursue such a partner through foreign courts, and a dishonest one could simply stay away from the next gathering. The fairs' answer was not stronger law but memory, for officials recorded disputes, and a merchant who defaulted could be barred from every future fair. Exclusion worked only because the fairs mattered so much; a market that traders could easily do without would have had no such hold on its members.
V01-M-017: For centuries, imperial China recruited many of its officials through written examinations open, in principle, to men of almost any family. The ideal was striking: office would go to learning rather than to birth, and a farmer's son might one day govern a province. In practice, years of study for the examinations required leisure and tutors, which wealthy families could buy far more easily than poor ones. Yet the system was not a mere disguise for privilege, since the occasional rise of a humble candidate kept the ideal believable to everyone. That belief may have been its most important product, binding ambitious men across a vast empire to the state that examined them.
V01-M-018: Economics textbooks usually assume that when the price of a good rises, people buy less of it. Some luxury goods seem to break this rule, because part of what their buyers want is the very fact that the item is expensive. A designer handbag is a familiar case, since one that anyone could afford would no longer signal its owner's wealth, and cutting its price might even reduce demand. The handbag's price, in other words, is not a cost its buyer tolerates but part of what she is paying for.
V01-M-019: Holding large stocks of parts ties up money and warehouse space, so many manufacturers learned to order parts only as they were needed. The savings were real, and for years the lean approach looked like simple good management. What it had quietly traded away was the cushion that let a factory keep running when a single supplier failed. When disruptions came, the missing cushion was felt at once, and firms with nearly empty shelves were often the first to halt production.
V01-M-020: Advocates of publishing every employee's salary argue that secrecy protects unfair gaps in pay, which survive only because nobody can see them. Openness does tend to narrow gaps that cannot be justified, since a manager must now defend each difference to everyone it affects. That pressure is indiscriminate, however, falling equally on differences that can be justified, and managers who dread explaining a large raise may simply decline to give it. Transparency, in short, does not so much make pay fair as make it uniform, and the two coincide only where performance is roughly equal.
V01-M-021: A company with a trusted brand is often tempted to stretch the name across new products, since customers already know and like it. The stretch saves money, because a familiar name needs far less advertising than an unknown one. It also carries a risk that is easy to overlook while sales of the new product are going well. Every product that bears the name teaches customers something about what the name means, and a cheap or unrelated product can teach them the wrong thing. A brand stretched too far may end up meaning nothing in particular, and so lose the very trust that made the stretch attractive.
V01-M-022: In the past, engineers straightened many winding rivers, cutting through their bends so that floodwater would be carried away faster. The straightened channels did move water quickly past the farms beside them, but they delivered it all the sooner to the towns downstream. Floods that the old meanders and marshes had once spread out and slowed now arrived downstream higher and faster, sometimes overwhelming defences built for gentler peaks. Some regions are therefore restoring the bends and wetlands that earlier generations of engineers removed, accepting slower drainage in return for safer towns.
V01-M-023: A field planted with a single high-yielding variety is easy to sow, tend and harvest, and in a good year it outproduces any mixed planting. Its uniformity is also its weakness, because a disease that can infect one plant in such a field can infect every plant in it. In a mixed field, by contrast, susceptible plants are separated by resistant ones, which slow the spread of the disease from neighbour to neighbour. The farmer who grows a mixture thus accepts a smaller harvest in good years in exchange for protection against the bad year that could destroy everything.
V01-M-024: A great volcanic eruption can cool the whole planet, but not, as one might expect, because of the ash that darkens the sky around it. Ash is heavy and falls out of the air within days or weeks, long before it could affect the climate of distant continents. The lasting effect comes from sulphur gases carried high into the stratosphere, where they form a fine haze of droplets that reflects sunlight back into space. Above the weather, with no rain to wash it out, this haze can linger for a year or more and spread around the globe. That is why an eruption in the tropics can be followed by failed harvests on the other side of the world in the following summer.
V01-M-025: When many published findings in a field fail to reappear on repetition, the natural suspicion is that some researchers have been careless or dishonest. A more troubling explanation needs no wrongdoing at all, only journals that prefer striking positive results to dull null ones. If many teams test unlikely ideas and only the lucky successes are printed, the literature will fill with flukes even if every study was conducted honestly. Repairing such a field, then, requires changing what gets published, not merely policing the people who publish it.
